280: Four important numbers on the disc
281: Match the diameter, thickness, bore size and maximum rated speed to the machine. Do not select an unsuitable diameter or a disc whose speed rating is lower than the machine's speed. Mounting and guarding must follow the machine's instructions exactly.

290: Start with the distances you actually measure
291: Identify the longest distance you normally measure. A tool's nominal range is defined under suitable test conditions. Bright light, dark or reflective surfaces and awkward angles can make readings difficult. Don't rely solely on the largest number on the box.
292: Range and accuracy are different specifications
293: Range is the measurable distance; accuracy is the stated deviation under defined conditions. Estimating room dimensions and installing fine details do not require the same performance. Consider accuracy alongside your measuring method, the device's front or rear reference point and the conditions stated in its manual.
295: Area and volume calculations, continuous measurement, memory and data transfer can simplify work. Start by listing your most frequent tasks. Extra functions without a practical need do not necessarily make a better choice.
297: Never direct a laser at anyone's eyes, and take care around reflective surfaces. Read the IP rating in the official manual: splash resistance is not the same as suitability for immersion. Maintain and, where needed, calibrate the tool as instructed.

304: Read the accuracy with its unit

307: Keep the contact surface and vials clean. After an impact or before precise work, check the reading using the manufacturer's recommended method. Magnets can make positioning on metal easier, but do not replace checking stability and reading accuracy.
